trails.title: Entrusted Visions
trails.description: People, then as now, nurtured dreams worth sharing.

content.text:
My Dearest Cousin Ladislas,

How oft thou art in my prayers. I trust with all my heart that Italy hath already begun to feel as home unto thee. I am told the folk there are warm of spirit and generous of hand; I can well believe thou hast found many a kindly friend upon thy path.

Marianne and I do prepare for a journey into Austria, and our hearts are full of longing. For there lieth, as thou hast spake so oft, the very heart of the new art. I yearn to lift mine eyes unto the golden tracery crowning the Secession Building, whilst Marianne doth dream of wandering through the galleries and little shops of the Wiener Werkstätte. We have set our minds also upon the Karlskirche—Fischer von Erlach's great Baroque church. They say its nineteen stained-glass windows shine as jewels and its nave holdeth a majesty not soon forgotten. Should any sketches from our travels serve thy studies, it would delight me to send them forth.

Our past words dwell yet within me. Marianne telleth me ever of the new age dawning—of electric light supplanting the gentle glow of candles, and of the darkness of our nights fading away. Yet, dear Ladislas, I still feel the nearness of the old ways. This age of machines hath left many unsettled and without refuge; soon they shall crave a quiet place wherein to kneel and seek God's comfort and counsel.

Then do I call to mind thy words, and my heart is moved—that our prayers must rise above the clamour of industry. And so do I begin to dream, with thee in my thoughts, of a church for this new century, yet still a haven for the soul. Though our cousin smileth at such fancies, her words have sown new imaginings in me, and I have begun to set them down in drawings. Mayhap to raise such a place would take ten, even fifteen years; yet it comforteth me to picture thee by my side when the time cometh, helping to bring our vision to life.

Thou art ever in my thoughts and ever in my prayers.

With all my love,
Agnès
April 2, 1914

items.text: An Unfulfilled Prophecy
Ladislas hasn't spoken a word since news of the ceasefire reached their sanctuary.
He's been kneeling at the altar for days, having eaten next to nothing. Always thin, he now looks more like a jagged stone obelisk than a man.

items.speaker: Female Gargoyle
items.text: What am I to do, my sweetie? He will not so much as touch the biscuits I baked for him. Never have I seen him in such a state.
The woman clasps her hands to her chest, worried but helpless.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Ladislas.
She gently calls out to him.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: The war has ended not as he foretold.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: It may take some time ere he is able to free himself of his guilt.

items.speaker: Female Gargoyle
items.text: Dear Ladislas, *sigh* keep thy heart in the Lord, for He shall forgive us, no matter how great our missteps.
The good and pious woman stops herself from saying more. There's no line of reasoning sufficient to break him from his watch.

items.speaker: Female Gargoyle
items.text: Marie, I beg thee do something. One way or another, we all must return to Rouen in the coming days.
She leaves without another word.
Sentinel comes to Ladislas's side but has no desire to interrupt his silent prayers. Her focus instead is on the statue of the crying girl.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Ladislas, you foretold that Agnès would return to herself come the end of the war.
She pulls out a handkerchief to softly clean the stone's unmoving face.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Yet she remains unchanged. Is there truly no way to revive our dear friend? Our family?
Once again, she receives only a humbling, guilt-ridden silence.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Marie?
She turns to the voice, finding it belongs to the woman that has become a regular visitor to their sanctuary. As usual, she brought food—this time some salami and dried cheese.
After handing off the supplies, Marsha marches straight toward her.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: What news from the front?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Some troops have already withdrawn. The rest will follow suit once the armistice is officially signed.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Ladislas ... He still won't eat?

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Just leave him be.
She doesn't let Marsha dwell on the matter, returning to her work dusting the statue.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: If you don't mind me asking, is this statue real?

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: What do you mean?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: I-I'm not sure how to put this into words properly. It's just that I've never seen her move.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Ah, now your words are clear.
She gathers her handkerchief and takes a deep breath, the cold, wet morning mist filling her lungs.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: This is Agnès, a distant cousin of mine. We share a great-grandmother.
She places her hand on Agnès's stone knee.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: We took residence together until 1914—both at our clan estate in the suburbs of Rouen and in my rented apartment in Paris.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: When the war broke out, I departed to join the army. Upon returning during my first leave, I found her in the cellar—it came to pass that, in my absence, she had turned herself to stone.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: She can stay in this form as she pleases?

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Only so long as her heart yet beats. Were she to turn to stone from within, she would be unable to restore her body to flesh.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: But Ladislas informed me of another possibility.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: He said Agnès's petrification was an extraordinary act of self-sacrifice.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: And that this sacrifice was also a prophecy: Gargoyles were not to coexist with this war.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: He said that a miracle would occur—that Agnès would be freed from her petrification. I thought it might have been true.
She glances toward Ladislas, still kneeling.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: But I suppose it was not. Agnès has shown no signs of recovery.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: There must be another way.
The Gargoyle shakes her head, disheartened.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: If only there were—if only I knew of one. But there is very little I know of our bloodline.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: While the young of my kin generally receive a traditional education from within the clan, my grandmother supported my decision to attend a secular school in my youth.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: I resided in a small rented apartment in Paris for some time, hoping to enroll at l'ENSAD—that was, until the war broke out.
Sentinel forces herself to look into Marsha's eyes.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: This war ... Well, you've seen the face of it. It takes but one shot to end a life, and this war has hurt millions. Friends, family, loved ones ... I have lost far too many.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Marie ...

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Forget it. Tell me, have you yet time today?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: What do you want to do?

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Take a stroll. I have spent far too much time in the monastery.
Windmill Plain
After a long journey, they return to the field once soaked in blood.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: A pilot?
Their earlier conversation still lingers.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Yes, that's what I wanted to be.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Why?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Many knights joined the air force at the time. They believed the sky to be the only battlefield that still maintained at least some semblance of knightly chivalry.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: It had more than the ground, at least, crawling through mud and digging trenches.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: I loathe airplanes. They're exceedingly difficult to withstand from the ground, and the engine noise.
She swallows the complaints, not wanting to sound bitter.
Marsha extends her arm over to her friend's back.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Relax, you don't need to fight them anymore. In fact, I'd wager you'll come to like traveling by plane in time.
She turns to the sea of grass rippling in the wind.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: The corpses that lay yonder—did you see them earlier?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: No. Perhaps Charon had already buried them.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Hah, most likely. He is an interesting fellow, if not strange.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: And kind, too. Without him, you and I would certainly have fought again at the graveyard.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Oh, that reminds me!
Suddenly, she bends down, rummaging in the roadside dirt.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: What?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: You threw a smoke grenade at me!

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Hey!

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Hahaha!
They laugh as they race down the dirt road, feeling more like children than soldiers for the moment, however brief.
They come to a halt before the windmill, its colossal gears interlocking and turning, like the breath of a slumbering ancient giant.
The slow creaking of the windmill becomes the only sound.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Marsha.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Hm?

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Are you leaving?

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: No. I have plenty of free time today.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: Not now, after the armistice. I know well that the Foundation has tasked you with keeping a watchful eye on me.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: It's not exactly like that.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: All is well. You may stay, so long as you do not lie.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: I shall even aid you should you require it. But do not attempt to persuade me to join the Foundation. I cannot abandon my family.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: I know that. I'll be leaving after the armistice is officially signed.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: *sigh*

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: It comes from the windmill.

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Sounds like a horse to me.

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: A horse?
They cautiously approach the windmill's entrance.
Sentinel moves ahead of Marsha, turning her body sideways, and hardens into stone to give a weighty push on the door.

items.speaker: War Horse
items.text: Neigh!

items.speaker: Marsha
items.text: Wow, what a beauty!

items.speaker: Sentinel
items.text: A horse indeed. What brings it here?
